title: ACT Reading — Practice Test 5
summary: A full timed enhanced-ACT Reading test: four original passages (a village literary narrative, paired natural science passages on the whale fossils of Wadi Al-Hitan, humanities on the Hilali epic of Upper Egypt and social science on Cairo's public bathhouses), 36 questions in 40 minutes, with a reason for every answer choice.

blocks.text: This is a full-length practice test for the **Reading section of the enhanced ACT**: **36 questions in 40 minutes**, four passages with 9 questions each. In the real test, **27 questions are scored** and one passage is unscored, but you will not know which one, so treat every passage as if it counts. **In this practice test, all 36 questions count.** All passages and questions are original.

rows: Natural Science — paired passages A and B

items: Sit in a quiet place, put your phone away and keep scrap paper and a pencil ready.
Do the whole section in one sitting. The timer starts when you press Start and the section ends automatically after 40 minutes.
Aim for about **10 minutes per passage**: roughly 3–4 minutes to read and map it, then about 6 minutes for its 9 questions.
For the paired passages, note each author's main claim in a few words before you answer the questions that compare them.
There is no penalty for wrong answers, so answer every question. If you are stuck, eliminate what you can, guess, mark it and move on.
The score shown at the end is a **practice percentage**, not an official ACT scaled score.

questions.p:
Passage I — Literary Narrative

LITERARY NARRATIVE: This passage is from an original memoir-style story. The narrator remembers the summer her father closed the village flour mill.

[1] The mill stood at the end of our lane, a square building of whitewashed brick with a tin roof that rang like a drum when it rained, which it almost never did. Inside, the air was always white. Flour settled on everything: on the belts and the great iron hopper, on the sacks waiting along the walls, on my father's eyebrows, so that for my whole childhood he looked older at work than he did at home.

[2] I came back from my first year at university in Cairo to find that he had decided to close it. He told me on the evening I arrived, in the same tone he used to tell me the price of tomatoes. Fewer families brought their own wheat to be ground now; most bought bags of flour from the shops in town, cheaper and finer than anything our old stones could produce. The engine needed a new part that cost more than the mill earned in a season. "A thing that does not pay," he said, "is a hobby. I am too old for hobbies."

[3] I offered to help during the last weeks, partly out of loyalty and partly, I admit, because I had nothing else to do. My job was the ledger, a thick green book in which my father recorded every sack that came through the door: the name of the family, the weight, the kind of grain, the fee. I had not opened it since I was a child, when I used to copy the names into my school notebook for practice. Now I turned its pages with a student's new seriousness, and I saw what I had never noticed before.

[4] Half the fees had never been paid. Beside many names, in my father's small, square handwriting, was a single word: "later." Some of these entries were years old. Umm Saber, who lived alone at the far end of the village, appeared every week for as far back as the book went—a small sack of maize, never more than five kilos—and beside every entry was the same word.

[5] I showed him the page, expecting him to be embarrassed or annoyed. He glanced at it and went on oiling a bearing. "She pays," he said.

[6] "Not according to this."

[7] "The book is for weight," he said. "It is not for everything."

[8] On the last day, the mill was busier than I had seen it in years. Word had spread, and people came who had not brought grain in a long time, some with sacks, some with nothing at all, as if they had come to a funeral and did not know what to bring. Men stood outside smoking and telling stories about the old engine, which had once, famously, caught fire during a wedding. Children ran in and out, white to the knees.

[9] Umm Saber came in the late afternoon with her small sack and a covered basket. My father ground the maize himself, slowly, and poured the flour into her cloth bag. She did not offer money, and he did not ask for it. Instead she lifted the cloth from the basket and gave him a round loaf, still warm, baked, she said, from last week's flour. He broke it in half and handed half to me, and we ate it standing in the doorway while she walked home along the canal. That evening my mother told me, as if it were the most ordinary thing in the world, that a loaf had arrived at our house every week for as long as she could remember.

[10] That night my father locked the door and gave me the key. I did not know what to do with it, so I kept it, and I have it still. When people ask me what my father did, I say that he ran a mill. It is true, but I have come to think, as he said of his ledger, that it is not everything.
questions.q: The passage is mainly about:
c: the reasons the narrator chose to study at a university in Cairo.
a long dispute between the father and Umm Saber over unpaid fees.
the narrator's discovery, during the mill's last weeks, that her father's work meant more than earning money.
the day the mill's old engine caught fire during a wedding.
questions.e: The narrator learns that the mill was about more than money. B invents a conflict that never happens.
ce: Off target: her studies are mentioned only to explain when she came home.
Contradicted: there is no dispute; the father says simply, 'She pays.'
Right: the ledger, Umm Saber's bread and the crowded last day all show her what the mill really meant.
Too narrow: the fire is a story the men tell in one sentence of paragraph 8.

Passage II — Natural Science (Paired Passages)

NATURAL SCIENCE: Passage A is from an original essay by a palaeontologist, Adel Nassif. Passage B is from an original essay by a museum curator, Salma Fikry. Both writers are fictional.

PASSAGE A — "Read Them Where They Lie"

[1] In the desert of Egypt's Fayoum region lies Wadi Al-Hitan, the Valley of the Whales. Scattered across its sand and pale rock are the fossil skeletons of early whales that lived around forty million years ago, when this part of Egypt lay beneath a warm, shallow sea. Some of the skeletons are more than fifteen metres long. A few still show something that no living whale has in visible form: small hind legs, complete with tiny knees and toes.

[2] These legs are why the valley matters so much. They are evidence of one of the great transitions in the history of life: the change from land-dwelling mammals to animals that live wholly in the sea. The ancestors of whales walked on four legs. By the time of the Wadi Al-Hitan whales, the front legs had become flippers and the back legs had shrunk until they were far too small to support the animal on land. A fossil showing that stage is worth more than a library of argument.

[3] I believe that most of the skeletons should stay where they are. A fossil removed from the rock loses part of its meaning. In place, it lies among the remains of the animals and plants that lived alongside it—sharks' teeth, sea cows, shells, the roots of mangrove trees—and within layers of rock that record the sea's slow retreat. A researcher who sees the skeleton in its setting can read the whole scene: what the water was like, what the whale ate, how its body came to rest. A visitor who walks the valley understands, in a way no museum label can teach, that this desert was once the bottom of the sea.

[4] This is why the valley was made a protected area and, in 2005, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and why visitors follow marked paths to skeletons left in the ground. The fossils are not hidden in a storeroom. They are part of the landscape, and the landscape is part of them.

PASSAGE B — "Bring Them Indoors"

[1] Wadi Al-Hitan is one of the finest fossil sites in the world, and I share my colleagues' pride in the decision to display skeletons where they were found. But I am uneasy about how long that display can last. The same wind that uncovered these bones is still blowing. Sand that has polished the rock for thousands of years will polish an exposed rib or vertebra just as patiently, and a fossil, unlike a living thing, cannot repair itself once it is worn away.

[2] The danger is not only the weather. Every year more visitors come, and although most follow the paths, it takes only one careless step, or one souvenir hunter, to destroy a delicate bone that survived forty million years. Shelters and ropes help. They do not solve the problem.

[3] My proposal is a compromise rather than a reversal. The most important skeletons—especially the rare ones with hind limbs—should be carefully excavated and moved to a museum where temperature, light and dust can be controlled, and where scientists can study them with instruments that cannot be carried into the desert. In their place, exact casts could be laid in the original positions, so that visitors still see a whale in the sand. Detailed records of the setting—photographs, maps, three-dimensional scans—would preserve much of what is lost when a bone leaves the rock.

[4] Some will say that a cast is only a copy and that a copy lacks the power of the real thing. That is true. But a real thing that has crumbled has no power at all. Our first duty is to make sure that the bones still exist for the next generation to argue about.

Passage III — Humanities

HUMANITIES: This passage is from an original essay about a tradition of epic poetry in Upper Egypt. The folklorist quoted is fictional.

[1] Late on a summer night in a village in Upper Egypt, a crowd sits on benches and mats around a man with a two-stringed fiddle. He has been singing for nearly two hours, and he is not close to the end. He will not reach the end tonight, or tomorrow night either. The story he is telling, the Sirat Bani Hilal, is so long that no one performs it from beginning to end in a single sitting; many performers say that the whole epic, sung completely, would fill weeks of evenings.

[2] The Sirat Bani Hilal tells of the Bani Hilal, an Arab tribe that, in the story, is driven by drought to leave the Arabian Peninsula and travel west through Egypt into North Africa. Its most famous hero is Abu Zayd al-Hilali, a warrior of great courage and cunning, whose adventures—battles, disguises, journeys, quarrels over honour and love—fill a large part of the epic. Behind the legend lies a real migration of Arab tribes into North Africa in the eleventh century, but the epic is not a history book. Over centuries of retelling it has gathered characters, episodes and meanings far beyond anything a chronicle would record.

[3] For most of its history, the epic has lived not on paper but in the voices of professional poets. In Upper Egypt these poets have traditionally learned it within families, son from father, beginning as boys who sit beside their elders at performances and absorb thousands of lines by hearing them again and again. They accompany themselves on the rababa, a simple fiddle whose body is made from a coconut shell, and much of the epic is sung in rhymed verse.

[4] What surprises many outsiders is that no two performances are the same. A poet does not recite a fixed text the way an actor speaks memorised lines. He knows the story, its scenes and a large store of traditional phrases, and from these he builds each performance anew. "The poet is not a recording," says the folklorist Hassan Darwish, who has spent years recording such performances. "He is a composer working in front of an audience, and the audience is part of the composition."

[5] The audience shapes the performance in direct ways. Listeners call out comments, laugh, argue with the characters and ask for favourite episodes. A good poet notices who is present and adjusts: he may lengthen a battle scene for an excited crowd of young men, add a joke about a well-known local family, or slow down for an emotional parting when older listeners are moved. One of Darwish's recordings captures the same poet singing the same episode on two nights a week apart; the second version is nearly twice as long, because on that night, the poet later explained, "they were listening well."

[6] This flexibility is the source of the epic's survival. A fixed text can be preserved, but it can also grow stale; a living performance stays connected to the people who hear it. Yet the same flexibility makes the tradition fragile. Because the epic exists in the memories of performers rather than in a single authoritative book, it depends on each generation finding young people willing to spend years learning it. In recent decades, as audiences have turned to television and other entertainment, fewer sons have followed their fathers into the profession.

[7] Recognition has come from outside. In 2003, UNESCO proclaimed the Hilali epic a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity, and researchers have recorded many hours of performances. Darwish welcomes the recordings but warns against mistaking them for the tradition itself. "A recording keeps one night," he says. "The epic was never one night. It was every night, different each time, with whoever happened to be sitting on the benches."

[8] Perhaps that is the best way to understand the Sirat Bani Hilal: not as a text that poets remember, but as a conversation between a poet and his listeners that has lasted for centuries and has never been quite the same twice.

Passage IV — Social Science

SOCIAL SCIENCE: This passage is from an original article about the social history of the public bathhouses of Cairo. The historian quoted is fictional.

[1] For centuries, one of the most important buildings in a Cairo neighbourhood was one that many of today's residents have never entered: the hammam, or public bathhouse. From the outside it was often modest, marked by a decorated doorway and, on the roof, a cluster of small domes set with pieces of glass that let daylight fall in soft circles onto the steam below. Inside, a visitor passed through a series of rooms, each warmer than the last, from a cool entrance hall where people undressed and rested to a hot, steamy chamber where they washed and were scrubbed.

[2] In a city where few homes had running water, the hammam met a basic need. Washing thoroughly at home meant carrying and heating large amounts of water, a heavy and slow task. At the hammam, water was heated in great quantities over a furnace fed with whatever fuel could be found, and the cost of a visit was within reach of most families.

[3] But the historian Mona El-Gamal argues that to see the hammam only as a place for washing is to miss most of its meaning. "People did not go to the hammam simply to get clean," she writes. "They went to spend time." A visit could last several hours. Men met friends, discussed business and heard the news of the quarter. Women, who used the bath at separate hours or on separate days, often treated their visit as a social outing, bringing food, children and conversation and staying for much of the day. For many women, El-Gamal notes, the hammam was one of the few places outside the home where they could gather freely with people who were not relatives.

[4] The hammam also marked important moments in life. Before a wedding, a bride typically went to the bathhouse with her female relatives and friends in a celebration of its own, with singing and special foods. Similar visits could mark recovery from an illness or the return from a long journey. In this way, El-Gamal argues, the bathhouse was a stage for the community's rituals as well as for its everyday routines.

[5] The hammam's decline came gradually. From the late nineteenth century onward, piped water reached more and more Cairo homes, and private bathrooms became common, first among the wealthy and then more widely. Each new bathroom removed one more reason to visit the public bath. At the same time, new places for socialising—clubs, cinemas and, later, cafés where women could meet—took over parts of its social role. Many hammams closed; their buildings were turned into workshops or storerooms, or simply left empty.

[6] El-Gamal is careful not to tell this story as one of simple loss. Running water at home, she points out, brought real benefits, especially for health and for the women and girls who had once carried water every day. "Nobody should be nostalgic about hauling buckets," she writes. What was lost was not the washing but the gathering: a regular, shared, unhurried place that brought together people of different ages and backgrounds and that belonged to the whole neighbourhood.

[7] A small number of historic hammams in Cairo still operate, and several others have been restored as monuments. Some visitors come out of curiosity, others out of long habit. El-Gamal sees in them less a relic than a question for modern cities. "We gave every home its own bathroom," she writes, "and that was right. But we never asked what would replace the room where the neighbourhood used to meet."
